faq.a: It directly visualises reflux during voiding and grades severity, which cannot be reliably inferred from ultrasound alone.
faq.q: Why is VCUG still the gold standard despite radiation?

faq.a: Yes, especially low‑grade VUR in children under 5 years; resolution rates decline with higher grades and older age.
Not always; some patients respond to strict infection control, but surgery is recommended if infections persist or renal scarring progresses.
faq.q: Is surgical correction always needed for high‑grade VUR?

exam: A 2‑year‑old with three febrile UTIs in 6 months – what is the next investigative step and why? — Perform VCUG to grade reflux; recurrent febrile UTIs in this age strongly suggest VUR.

How does primary VUR differ pathophysiologically from reflux secondary to posterior urethral valves? — Primary VUR is a congenital ureterovesical junction defect; secondary reflux results from increased bladder pressure due to obstruction.

A child with grade III VUR and a recent UTI is on prophylaxis but develops another infection – what management change is indicated? — Escalate to surgical correction (ureteric reimplantation) because breakthrough infection indicates prophylaxis failure.
Explain why a normal renal ultrasound does not rule out VUR. — Ultrasound assesses anatomy but cannot demonstrate urine flow reversal; VCUG is required to detect reflux.

In a low‑resource setting where VCUG is unavailable, what alternative test can be used and what are its limitations? — Radionuclide cystography can detect reflux with less radiation but provides no anatomic detail and may miss low‑grade reflux.
What are the long‑term renal complications of untreated high‑grade VUR? — Progressive renal scarring, hypertension, proteinuria, and eventual chronic kidney disease.

Why is long‑term trimethoprim‑sulfamethoxazole prophylaxis sometimes avoided in East African clinics? — Poor adherence, risk of resistance, and limited drug supply make it less reliable; focus shifts to prompt infection treatment.

Differentiate the clinical clues that point toward posterior urethral valves rather than VUR in a male infant. — Severe urinary stream obstruction, palpable bladder, and hydronephrosis without recurrent infection suggest valves; VUR presents mainly with febrile UTIs.
ai.title: Vesicoureteric Reflux in Children
ai.subject: Paediatrics
ai.summary: Vesicoureteric reflux (VUR) is the backward flow of urine from the bladder into the ureters and kidneys, predisposing to infection and renal damage. Diagnosis relies on imaging, staging guides management, and low‑resource settings require pragmatic use of available tests.

b: Diagnosed by imaging that demonstrates reflux during voiding
Requires at least one documented episode of reflux on study
sections.p: VUR is the abnormal retrograde passage of urine from the bladder into the ureter and renal pelvis, caused by a congenital or acquired defect in the ureterovesical junction.

t.b: Does urine flow back into ureters? – Positive shows reflux, grade 1‑5; negative essentially excludes VUR
Are kidneys enlarged or scarred? – Detects hydronephrosis, scarring, or congenital anomalies; normal does not rule out VUR
Is there cortical scarring? – Shows functional loss; if unavailable, rely on ultrasound and clinical course

b: Grade I: reflux into ureter only
Grade II: reflux into renal pelvis without dilation
Grade III: mild dilation of ureter and pelvis
Grade IV: moderate dilation and tortuosity
Grade V: severe dilation, tortuosity, and loss of papillary impression
sections.p: The International Reflux Study grades VUR from I (mild) to V (severe) based on the extent of reflux and ureteral dilation seen on VCUG.

b: Primary congenital ureterovesical junction incompetence
Posterior urethral valves (boys) – lower urinary tract obstruction
Neurogenic bladder (spina bifida)
Pelvi‑ureteric junction obstruction (can coexist)
Severe urinary tract infection (UTI) causing transient reflux
sections.p: Most VUR is primary, due to a congenital defect in the intramural ureter. Secondary VUR follows obstruction or infection, which are common in low‑resource settings.

b: Recurrent febrile UTI, especially <5 years
New onset hypertension in older children (renal scarring)
Abdominal/flank pain if pyelonephritis develops
sections.p: Children often present with recurrent febrile UTIs, poor growth, or incidentally on imaging for other reasons. Infants may have nonspecific irritability or failure to thrive.
Imaging is central; urine culture guides infection treatment. In low‑resource hospitals, prioritize bedside ultrasound and targeted VCUG.

t.b: Is a bacterial infection present? – Guides antibiotics; a sterile culture with symptoms suggests non‑infectious cause
Is there hydronephrosis or scarring? – Detects structural changes; if unavailable, proceed to VCUG based on clinical suspicion
Does reflux occur and what grade? – Determines severity; if VCUG not available, consider radionuclide cystography if feasible

b: Repeated febrile UTI despite treatment
Progressive renal scarring on imaging
New hypertension or proteinuria
sections.p: Uncontrolled reflux can lead to renal scarring, hypertension, and chronic kidney disease.

b: Acute UTI: start empiric broad‑spectrum antibiotic (e.g., ceftriaxone) pending culture
Low‑grade VUR (I‑II) in children <5 years: prophylactic low‑dose trimethoprim‑sulfamethoxazole if adherence possible
Higher grades (III‑V) or breakthrough infections: consider ureteric reimplantation or endoscopic Deflux injection
Avoid long‑term prophylaxis in poor adherence settings; prioritize prompt treatment of each infection
sections.p: Treat infection first, then address reflux based on grade, age, and renal damage. Surgical correction is reserved for high grades or failed medical therapy.

b: Repeat urine culture after each infection
Ultrasound at 6‑month intervals if scarring suspected
VCUG only if recurrent infection or worsening ultrasound findings
Educate caregivers on hygiene, hydration, and early fever reporting
sections.p: Regular monitoring prevents irreversible renal damage. In low‑resource settings, schedule follow‑up based on clinical events rather than routine imaging.

b: Posterior urethral valves – obstructive, mainly in boys
Neurogenic bladder – functional obstruction
Renal calculi – cause obstruction and pain
sections.p: Conditions that also cause recurrent UTIs or hydronephrosis can be mistaken for VUR.

b: Normal ultrasound does not exclude VUR; VCUG is required for definitive diagnosis
Negative urine culture after antibiotics may miss a persistent infection
sections.p: Imaging and labs may give false reassurance if interpreted without clinical context.

whenToSeekHelp: Fever >38 °C with dysuria or flank pain
Persistent vomiting, lethargy, or decreased urine output
New onset hypertension or swelling of the face/legs
